title: Did Dinosaurs Snack on Seaweed?
summary: Dinosaurs near ancient coasts may have snacked on seaweed. New research says ocean food washed onto beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey more than 100 million years ago. Scientists call this marine subsidization, which helps most when land food is scarce, such as in droughts. The researchers looked at chemical fingerprints in fossils. Plants hold two forms of carbon, called isotopes: light carbon-12 and heavy carbon-13. As animals eat, the carbon mark of their food ends up in their tooth enamel. The team studied coastal fossils near the Western Interior Seaway and the old Gulf of Mexico coast. Coastal fossils had higher carbon values than fossils from farther inland. The fossils formed in the early Albian, about 113 to 107 million years ago, and the early Cenomanian, about 100 to 96 million years ago. This is the first evidence of marine subsidization in old ecosystems. Dr. Clayton Forster of the University of Arkansas said ocean nutrients passed up the food chain to dinosaurs, crocodiles, turtles and fish.
why_it_matters: It shows how food from the sea and food from the land can be linked, just like the food you eat can come from many different places.

background_read: Dinosaurs lived on land, but food from the sea could also reach them when ocean food washed onto beaches.
Plants and animals carry tiny chemical marks from what they eat, and those marks can stay in fossils such as teeth.
By studying those marks, scientists can learn what ancient animals ate and how land and sea food were linked.
Article_Structure: WHO: Researchers studying fossils, including Dr. Clayton Forster of the University of Arkansas.
WHAT: They found the first evidence that ocean food washed onto beaches helped feed dinosaurs and their prey.
WHERE: Near ancient coasts by the Western Interior Seaway and the old Gulf of Mexico coast.
WHY: Ocean food helped most when land food was scarce, such as in droughts, and its nutrients passed up the food chain.
